statement: A list of numbers starts with 14. Each next number is half of the one before if that one is even, and 5 more than it if it is odd. So the list begins 14, 7, 12, 6, ... What is the 100th number in the list?

choices.misconception: I counted 4 numbers before the loop instead of 3, so 96 numbers were left, a whole number of loops, and I took the last loop number.
I counted 14 as the 0th number, so I really found the 101st number in the list.
I divided 100 by 6 and took the 4th number of the loop 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1, forgetting the 3 numbers that come before the loop starts.
I thought the whole list from 14 down to 1 repeats every 9 numbers, so the 100th number is the same as the 1st.

hints: Keep writing the list until a number comes back.
Once a number repeats, the list goes round the same loop for ever. Find where the loop starts and how long it is, then use a remainder, remembering the numbers before the loop.
The list is 14, 7, 12 and then the block 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1 repeats. The loop starts at the 4th number, so the 100th number is the 97th number of the looping part.

solutions.reliable: Write the list: 14, 7, 12, 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1, 6, 3, ... After 1 comes 1 + 5 = 6, so from the 4th number on, the block 6, 3, 8, 4, 2, 1 repeats every 6 numbers. The first 3 numbers are outside the loop, so the 100th number is the 97th number of the looping part. Since 97 = 16 x 6 + 1, it is the first number of the block, 6. The transferable idea: when a list settles into a loop, count positions from where the loop starts, not from the start of the list.
solutions.elegant: The 4th, 10th, 16th, ... numbers are all 6, one every 6 places. Since 100 = 4 + 16 x 6, the 100th number is one of them, so it is 6.

whyOnTest: Cycle questions get harder when a list takes a few steps to settle into its loop, and counting from the start of the loop is the skill being tested.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
